subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
When Wanjiru became team lead at the Nairobi call centre, she printed one line and stuck it on her monitor: What's in their way today?
On Monday it was the headsets. Half of them crackled, and the team had complained for a year. She spent two days on emails and a trip to the supplier, and on Thursday new ones arrived. Nobody made a speech about it. The complaints just stopped.
Mina, who had joined only in March, was good with angry callers. Wanjiru asked her to run the Friday training for the new hires, and sat at the back taking notes.
In the monthly report to the directors, Wanjiru listed every name of who had solved what.
She still ate lunch with her old shift, on the steps outside, with chapati and beans from the kiosk. Some days, they told her things she would never hear in a meeting.

qa.q: What line did Wanjiru stick on her monitor?
qa.a: What's in their way today?

qa.q: How might Mina have felt when asked to run the Friday training?
qa.a: Mina probably felt trusted and proud, since a newer team member was given a real chance to lead.

qa.q: Which of Wanjiru's habits builds lasting respect, and why?
qa.a: Fixing real obstacles like the headsets, crediting names in the report and staying close to old colleagues shows she leads by serving, not by position.

qa.q: What is it like for Wanjiru's old shift to still share lunch with her?
qa.a: They feel she hasn't left them behind, so they trust her with honest news she wouldn't hear in meetings.

grounding: It shows a leader treating the role as clearing obstacles and growing others, crediting the team and staying close to former peers.

passage:
The district library's reading room smelled of old paper and phenyl. Santosh had been senior librarian for eight months, and the staff still called him by his first name, which was how he wanted it.
His first act had been small: getting the broken scanner fixed, which had taken four letters to the municipal office and one long wait outside an officer's door. Hansa, the youngest assistant, had been printing forms by hand for a year. Now she didn't.
Hansa loved children's books, so he asked her to start a Saturday reading club. He helped arrange chairs the first week, then stepped back. By the third month forty children came.
At the annual function, when the collector praised the library, Santosh said, 'Please ask Hansa about the reading club. And Mr Pillai kept the catalogue alive.'
At one o'clock he still opened his tiffin at the old staff table.

qa.q: How many children came to the reading club by the third month?
qa.a: Forty children came by the third month.

qa.q: Why might Santosh want the staff to keep calling him by his first name?
qa.a: He seems content to stay one of the team and not set himself above his old colleagues.

qa.q: What did Santosh's approach to leading get right?
qa.a: He cleared real obstacles like the scanner, gave Hansa room to grow, and credited others publicly, which earns lasting respect.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel when Santosh sends the collector to ask her about the reading club?
qa.a: Hansa may feel seen and proud, knowing her work is credited to her and not taken by the boss.

grounding: It shows a leader clearing obstacles, growing a junior colleague, crediting the team and staying close to former peers.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Dear Salma,
You once told me a lead's real job is to be a good plumber: find what's blocked and clear it. I didn't get it when you said it. I think I do now.
When I took over the team in January, I spent the first month in meetings making decisions. The team got quieter. So I changed. Every Monday I now ask everyone one question: what's in your way this week? Last week it was a broken test server, a vendor who wasn't replying, and Ramesh's leave that kept getting stuck in approval. I spent my week on those three things. Nothing glamorous.
When the director praised our release, I named the four people who built it. I still eat lunch with the old gang on Thursdays; they tease me more than ever.
Ramesh runs the stand-ups now, and he's better at it than I was.
Thank you for the plumbing lesson.
Shankar

qa.q: What question does Shankar ask every Monday?
qa.a: What's in your way this week?

qa.q: How does Shankar seem to feel about the role now?
qa.a: Shankar seems settled and content, finding meaning in clearing blockages rather than in making every decision.

qa.q: Which of Shankar's habits builds the most lasting authority, and why?
qa.a: Clearing the team's blockers and naming the four builders to the director, because it earns trust through service, not position.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Shankar's leadership?
qa.a: Ramesh likely feels supported and trusted, since Shankar fixed the stuck leave and handed over the stand-ups.

grounding: A lead reframes the role as clearing obstacles and growing others, credits the team and stays close to old peers.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Gurleen, you've just been made lead, so let me tell you what I'd do differently if I started again. For my first three months I thought leading meant being the smartest person in the room. My team went quiet. Nobody told me when things went wrong.
What changed it was small. I started ending every one-to-one with, "What can I get out of your way?" Once it was a laptop that kept crashing. Once it was a client who kept calling my junior at midnight. I dealt with those things. That was the job.
I also stopped saying "I" in reports. It's "Neeraj built this, Shabnam tested that." And I still sit at our old table at lunch, where I sat as a junior, because those people tell me the truth.
A title gets people to listen for a week. What I do for them gets them to listen for years. I'm Pooja, and that's the one leadership lesson I really trust.

qa.q: What question does Pooja end every one-to-one with?
qa.a: What can I get out of your way?

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when the team went quiet in the early months?
qa.a: Pooja felt isolated and uneasy, since nobody said when things went wrong.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurleen based on Pooja's story?
qa.a: Start by asking what's in people's way, credit them by name, and keep sitting with former peers who will tell the truth.

qa.q: How might Neeraj and Shabnam feel seeing their names in the reports?
qa.a: They likely feel valued and seen, which makes them more willing to give their best.

grounding: A lead describes shifting from being the smartest in the room to removing obstacles, crediting the team and staying close to old peers.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
When Eshaan became our lead, I braced myself. I'd seen promotions change people.
The first Monday he didn't give a speech. He went round the room asking, "What's slowing you down?" Vinita said travel approvals took three weeks. By Thursday they took two days; he had sat with finance until it was fixed.
When our project won the regional award, he stood at the side of the stage and nudged Vinita forward to accept it, since she had designed the core model. I heard him tell the director, "I mostly got out of their way."
He still plays carrom with us in the break room at five, and still loses to the interns. Last month two people from other teams asked to transfer into ours.
I don't know if he planned any of this. From outside, it just looks like he keeps working for us, and we keep working harder for him.

qa.q: How long did travel approvals take before Eshaan fixed them?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have felt nudging Vinita forward on stage?
qa.a: He probably felt proud of the team and content to stay in the background, seeing his role as serving them.

qa.q: Which of Eshaan's actions best shows authority earned through service?
qa.a: Sitting with finance until travel approvals were fixed, because it removed a real obstacle for the team.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel accepting the award?
qa.a: Vinita likely feels honoured and trusted, credited for the model she designed instead of being hidden behind the lead 😊

grounding: A team member observes a new lead who clears obstacles, credits others and stays close to old peers, earning lasting respect.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Week one: Uma, three months into leading the clinic's front-desk team, asked each person the same question. "What's the one thing that wastes your time?" Ujjwal, who had shared a desk with her for two years, said the appointment printer jammed every morning and nobody had fixed it.
Week two: Uma spent Tuesday afternoon on the phone with the supplier until a new printer arrived. At the monthly review, the manager praised the shorter queues. Uma said, "Ujjwal redesigned the token system. That's why." Ujjwal went red and grinned into his tea.
Week four: Uma still ate lunch at the old corner table with Ujjwal and the others, and she asked Ujjwal to train the two new staff. When a patient shouted at the counter, it was Ujjwal who stepped in first, calm and steady, and Uma let him.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say wasted time every morning?
qa.a: Ujjwal said the appointment printer jammed every morning and nobody had fixed it.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Uma credited him at the review?
qa.a: He felt proud and a little embarrassed, which shows when he goes red and grins into his tea.

qa.q: What could Uma keep doing so the team keeps growing?
qa.a: She could keep asking what blocks people's work, fix those things, and hand real responsibility, like training new staff, to people like Ujjwal.

qa.q: How might the two new staff see Uma's way of leading?
qa.a: They would likely see a lead who stays close to her team and trusts them, which makes them more willing to learn from Ujjwal and speak up.

grounding: Shows a leader treating the role as removing obstacles and growing others, giving credit and staying close to former peers, and the respect that grows from it.
